analysis.one_liner: Requires packaged foods to list fat, saturated fat, sodium, and cholesterol on their labels.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: referred to a House subcommittee on May 8, 1989, it sat there with no hearings or markup recorded until the two-year Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required nearly all packaged foods containing fat, cholesterol, or sodium to state on the label the percentage of calories from fat, total fat broken into saturated, polyunsaturated, and monounsaturated fat, sodium, and cholesterol per serving. It was pitched as a heart-disease prevention measure, since federal health authorities had consensus that Americans eat too much fat, cholesterol, and salt but current labels often don't reveal them. It was introduced in April 1989, sent to a House subcommittee, and never came up for a vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Shoppers buying packaged foods. At the time, nearly half of processed, packaged foods regulated by the FDA carried no nutrition labeling at all, and even labeled products often omitted fat, sodium, or cholesterol details. The bill would have forced clear, standardized disclosure of the nutrients most tied to heart disease, on every covered product, in a format consumers could understand in the context of a daily diet.

how_it_helps.text: Would require any packaged food containing fat, cholesterol, or sodium to disclose calories from fat, total fat with its saturated, polyunsaturated, and monounsaturated breakdown, sodium, and cholesterol per serving.

Closes a real information gap: the bill's findings state that nearly half of processed, packaged foods regulated by the FDA carried no nutrition labeling at the time, and existing labels often omitted the very nutrients health authorities told Americans to limit.

Would require the disclosures to be presented so consumers can readily observe and comprehend them and understand each nutrient's significance in the context of the total daily diet, addressing confusing label formats and potentially misleading health claims.

Would put label information in line with federal health advice: the bill cites the Surgeon General, NIH, and the National Academy of Sciences recommending Americans cut total fat to 30% or less of calories, saturated fat below 10%, cholesterol below 300 mg daily, and salt to 6 grams, to reduce coronary heart disease risk.

analysis.who_pays: Packaged food manufacturers, who would have had one year from enactment to redesign and print new labels listing fat, sodium, and cholesterol content for every covered product. Those compliance costs would likely be passed partly into consumer prices, though they are one-time label changes rather than ongoing costs.

drawbacks.text: Imposes a federal labeling mandate on essentially every packaged food containing fat, cholesterol, or sodium — an extremely broad set of products — requiring new label design and printing within one year of enactment, a tight deadline that would fall hardest on smaller producers.

Labels alone do not change what people eat; the bill's own premise is that diet-related disease is driven by consumption, and a skeptic could argue that mandated disclosures are a modest tool against heart disease compared to its compliance cost across the whole packaged-food industry.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit side is broad and durable: standardized disclosure of the nutrients most linked to heart disease, on every covered product, replacing a patchwork in which nearly half of packaged foods had no nutrition label. The costs are real but bounded — one-time label redesign and printing within a year. The bill is simple and does not set food standards or ban anything; its main design risk is the one-year compliance deadline. On balance the gains to consumers outweigh the compliance burden, which is why its death in committee without even a hearing is notable.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced, sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, then to its health subcommittee, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Joe Moakley introduced the bill on April 18, 1989, joined by Rep. James Traficant, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day.
It gained 49 cosponsors — 46 Democrats and 3 Republicans — but the Energy and Commerce Committee took no action beyond referring it to the Subcommittee on Health and the Environment on May 8, 1989.
No further action is recorded: the bill never received a subcommittee vote, a committee markup, or a floor vote, and it died when the 101st Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Packaged food manufacturers came out ahead: they avoided mandatory on-label disclosure of fat, saturated fat, sodium, and cholesterol content for the rest of the Congress, and kept discretion over whether to label at all and which health claims to make.

for.name: Rep. Joe Moakley
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on April 18, 1989, framing mandatory nutrition disclosure as a heart-disease reduction measure.

for.name: Rep. James Traficant
for.what_they_did: Joined Moakley in introducing the bill at introduction.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral on April 18, 1989, and never reported it; its only recorded action was sending the bill to a subcommittee on May 8, 1989.

against.name: Subcommittee on Health and the Environment
against.role: House Energy and Commerce subcommittee that received the referral
against.what_they_did: Held the bill from May 8, 1989 onward; no hearing, markup, or vote on it appears in the record for the remainder of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: All 49 cosponsors listed were 46 Democrats and 3 Republicans, so early support was heavily but not entirely Democratic; there was never a roll-call vote, so the final partisan split is unknown.

industries.note: The bill would have forced every covered product to disclose calories from fat, fat breakdown, sodium, and cholesterol on the label within a year. The industry's interest in the bill's failure was keeping labeling voluntary — the bill's findings note nearly half of packaged foods then carried no nutrition labeling — which is the opposite of shoppers' interest in knowing what is in their food.
